title: The Wiles of Reptiles
bodyHtml:
Here are eight sentences in Dime.1 The first seven are given along with their English translations.

1.guurafis kénim šuiftinThe crocodiles deceived them.
2.ʔaté goštú gúdúmubim ʔóllóχ kúbitI carried a tall man slowly.
3.wúdúr čək’k’ind s’áámisim yefinA small girl saw the eagle.
4.guuru bášmubis ʔeftafim gáʔinThe fearful crocodile bit birds.
5.zimaf daχidis zití s’anubim ʔólóχ maddinThe strong chiefs helped a black ox quickly.
6.kété ʔámzi kitimindim kóχinThey loved a selfish woman.
7.goštáf koχsimid s’ááme koχsimubisim šiʔinPleasant men washed the pleasant eagle.
8.ʔámzaf gúdúmidis zime bášmubim kúbin

Notes:

In this problem, an accent above a vowel (e.g., in “kété”) indicates that the vowel has high tone. Unmarked vowels have low tone. A consonant or vowel written twice in a row (e.g., in “guurafis”) is pronounced for a longer time by the speaker. An apostrophe following a consonant (e.g., in “s’anubim”) indicates that the consonant is pronounced ejectively (i.e., with air pressure produced in the throat instead of the lungs).

The six sentences below were uttered by a linguist who had been trying to learn Dime. Unfortunately, only three of them were fully understood by native speakers; the other three were deemed incorrect, meaning they contained mistakes or were not understood at all.

(a) ʔaté s’ááme s’anubim kóχin

  • W. The sentence is correct as is (change nothing).
  • X. Change “kóχin” to “kóχit”.
  • Y. Change “s’anubim” to “s’anudim”.
  • Z. Change “s’ááme” to “s’áámaf”.

(b) wúdúraf gúdúmid zime kitimubisim ʔóllóχ šuiftin

  • W. The sentence is correct as is (change nothing).
  • X. Change “wúdúraf gúdúmid” to “wúdúrid gúdúmaf”.
  • Y. Change “šuiftin” to “šuiftit”.
  • Z. Change “ʔóllóχ” to “ʔámzi”.

(c) goštú zitáfisim koχsim yefin

  • W. The sentence is correct as is (change nothing).
  • X. Change “goštú zitáfisim” to “goštáfis zitáfid”.
  • Y. Change “zitáfisim” to “zitidim”.
  • Z. Change “zitáfisim koχsim” to “zitáf koχsimidisim”.

(d) wúdúris guuru s’anisubim maddin

  • W. The sentence is correct as is (change nothing).
  • X. Change “s’anisubim” to “s’anindisim”.
  • Y. Change “s’anisubim” to “s’anubisim”.
  • Z. Change “s’anisubim” to “s’anisim”.

(e) goštú čək’k’ubis kénim šiʔin

  • W. The sentence is correct as is (change nothing).
  • X. Change “čək’k’ubis kénim” to “čək’k’im kété”.
  • Y. Change “goštú čək’k’ubis” to “goštaf čək’k’idis”.
  • Z. Change “šiʔin” to “šiʔit”.

(f) kété s’ááme bášmubisim ʔólóχ gáʔin

  • W. The sentence is correct as is (change nothing).
  • X. Change “ʔólóχ” to “ʔámzi”.
  • Y. Change “s’ááme” to “s’áámim”.
  • Z. Change “bášmubisim” to “bášmidisim”.

1 Dime is an Afroasiatic language spoken in Ethiopia. Estimates of the number of speakers of Dime vary from a few hundred, on the low end, up to a few thousand; all studies agree, however, that the number of speakers is decreasing, and the language is threatened with extinction. Dime speakers live in a series of farming communities located along a mountain range and have relatively little contact with outside groups. The speakers are skilled metal producers, with techniques for extracting and smelting ores forming an important part of their traditional cultural knowledge.

hints.text: Start by lining up the word order. In every sentence the subject comes first, then the object, then the verb, and inside a noun phrase the noun comes before its adjective. Once you know which chunk is subject and which is object, compare the endings that get piled onto the ends of those chunks.

Each noun phrase carries up to three pieces of information in a fixed order: gender/number first, then definiteness ("the" versus "a"), then case (whether it is the object). The key discovery is that these endings attach to the noun only when there is no adjective; when an adjective follows the noun, the endings move onto the adjective, and the noun keeps just a plural marker if it is plural. The verb also ends differently depending on whether the subject is "I" or a third person.

Work sentence 1 as a model: guurafis kénim šuiftin, "The crocodiles deceived them." There is no adjective, so all the endings sit on the noun: guura (crocodile) + af (plural) + is (definite), and no object ending because it is the subject. Compare sentence 4, guuru bášmubis, where the same word for crocodile appears bare and the endings -ub (masculine singular) and -is (definite) sit on the adjective bášm- instead. Now try the same slot-by-slot analysis on the sentences the linguist produced.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: find the skeleton of a sentence

Compare sentence 4: guuru bášmubis ʔeftafim gáʔin = "The fearful crocodile bit birds." The word for the biter comes first, the bitten things second, and the verb last. That is Subject - Object - Verb order (SOV). Inside the phrase "the fearful crocodile" the noun (guuru, crocodile) comes before the adjective (bášm-, fearful), so noun phrases are Noun - Adjective.

Sentences 2 and 5 show that an adverb such as ʔóllóχ "slowly" or ʔólóχ "quickly" sits just before the verb. Notice that these two words differ only in how long the ll is - length is meaningful in Dime.

Step 2: the verb endings

Every verb here ends in -i- plus a final consonant: šuift-i-n, kúb-i-t, yef-i-n. The -i- marks past tense. The final consonant agrees with the subject: -t when the subject is "I" (ʔaté ... kúbit "I carried"), -n when the subject is a third person ("the crocodiles", "they", "a girl").

Step 3: the noun-phrase endings

When there is no adjective, the endings stack on the noun in a fixed order:

  • gender/number: -af plural, nothing for singular
  • definiteness: -is for "the", nothing for "a"
  • case: -im when the phrase is the object, nothing when it is the subject

So guura-af-is gives guurafis "the crocodiles" (subject), and ʔefta-af-im gives ʔeftafim "birds" (object, indefinite). Also compare s’ááme "eagle" in sentence 7 with s’áám-is-im "the eagle (object)" in sentence 3: the final vowel of the root drops before an ending.

When an adjective is present, the endings move onto the adjective, and the noun keeps only its plural marker:

  • gender/number on the adjective: -ub masculine singular, -ind feminine singular, -id plural
  • then -is definite, then -im accusative, as before

Examples: guuru bášm-ub-is "the fearful crocodile" (subject, masculine singular); ʔámzi kitim-ind-im "a selfish woman" (object, feminine singular); zimaf daχ-id-is "the strong chiefs" (noun keeps plural -af, adjective takes plural -id plus definite -is). Animals and chiefs count as masculine by default. One extra detail: a noun whose singular ends in a high-tone vowel keeps that high tone in its plural, so goštú "man" becomes goštáf "men" (not goštaf).

Step 4: the vocabulary

Nouns: guura crocodile, ʔefta bird, s’ááme eagle, wúdúr girl, goštú man, ʔámzi woman, zime chief, zití ox. Pronouns: ʔaté I, kété they, kénim them. Adjectives: gúdúm tall, čək’k’ small, bášm fearful, kitim selfish, s’an black, daχ strong, koχsim pleasant. Verbs: šuift- deceive, kúb- carry, yef- see, gáʔ- bite, madd- help, kóχ- love, šiʔ- wash.

Step 5: sentence 8

ʔámzaf gúdúmidis zime bášmubim kúbin: the subject is ʔámza-af "women" plus gúdúm-id-is "tall" (plural, definite, no object ending); the object is zime bášm-ub-im "a fearful chief" (masculine singular, indefinite, object); the verb kúb-i-n is past with a third-person subject. Hence: The tall women carried a fearful chief.

Step 6: judging the linguist's six sentences

(a) ʔaté s’ááme s’anubim kóχin: the subject is ʔaté "I", so the verb must end in -t, not -n. Option X fixes it: kóχit. Meaning: "I loved a black eagle."

(b) wúdúraf gúdúmid zime kitimubisim ʔóllóχ šuiftin: subject "tall girls" (plural, indefinite), object "the selfish chief" (masculine singular, definite, accusative), adverb "slowly", verb third person past. Everything fits, so option W. Meaning: "Tall girls deceived the selfish chief slowly."

(c) goštú zitáfisim koχsim yefin: the endings sit on the noun even though an adjective follows - not allowed. Option Z rebuilds the object as zitáf koχsimidisim (noun keeps plural -af; adjective takes plural + definite + accusative). Meaning: "A man saw the pleasant oxen."

(d) wúdúris guuru s’anisubim maddin: here the definite -is comes before the gender marker -ub, which is the wrong order. Option Y gives s’anubisim (gender, then definiteness, then case). Meaning: "The girl helped the black crocodile."

(e) goštú čək’k’ubis kénim šiʔin: "the small man" as subject, "them" as object, third-person past verb - all correct, so option W. Meaning: "The small man washed them." (Option Y fails because goštaf is missing the high tone that goštáf must keep.)

(f) kété s’ááme bášmubisim ʔólóχ gáʔin: "they" as subject, an eagle described as fearful as object, "quickly", third-person past verb - correct, so option W. The official translation is "They bit a fearful eagle quickly."
